doc.title: Ed Polcer interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998

title: The house band at Condon's and how it was led
summary: He names the band members (Jim Andrews, Balaban, Vic Dickenson, Tom Artin, Herb Hall, Bobby Gordon, Jack Maheu and the drummers), the sub policy and the shared leading.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: And who was in your house band while you were there?

Well the first house band involved Jimmy, most of the time Jim Andrews was our piano player and Red Balaban was the bass player. We went through several different drummers, Ronny Cole, Connie Kaye from the MJQ was our drummer for about three years believe it or not, played great drums, in our style, Danny DeImperio, a great drummer from upstate New York came in and did the last three years. I was the cornetist the whole time, the basic one. For a long period of — most of the time was Vic Dickinson on trombone until he got feeble or sick, around two years before the club closed. Tom Artin, a Princetonian friend of mine who I’d played with since 1955, he came in and replaced Vic, in fact Tom Artin in my estimation was one of the better trombone players in the country, not too many people know him. Went through several very good piano players, Herb Hall was the original one, Edmond Hall’s brother, he was there for three years with us. He was our original clarinetist and we had Bobby Gordon a very fine I would say Joe Marsala type, Pee Wee Russell influenced clarinetist, a real musician’s musician. He now plays in San Diego, California. And we finished with Jack Maheu, who came from, who I guess was one of the co-leaders of the Salt City Six from the Rochester area, Syracuse-Rochester, so he was the clarinetist for the last three years or so. So it was, and we had an agreement with anybody in the band that if you could get another gig elsewhere, a high paying gig or you wanted a night off, just call me and I would get a replacement. So it was almost very seldom that for two nights in a row we’d have exactly the same band, which kept the music kind of alive and you know you don’t get so used to playing with the same guys night after night, and each night could become a little different. Just change one out of six and the whole chemistry can change.
And you would just go up — would you go up on the stand and call the tunes as you felt, playing to the crowd somewhat?
That’s right. We ended up Red Balaban led the band pretty much three nights and I led it three. Most of the time early on he led it five or six nights and it evolved that I would

have the band on Monday nights. I tried changing it a little bit on Monday nights toward the end and had a few modern players, Lew Tabackin I remember working with him one night, Effie Resnick who had gotten quite modern on trombone. I was trying to present a little bit of a more modern flavor, but that was just my indulging myself. But yeah, we’d just go up on the stand and not give it that much thought. I’d look down the songlist, say hey we’ll do this, and if we had requests we’d play the requests. It was about as loose as it could get. The music spoke for itself really.
